⚡️🇺🇸 MicroVision has unveiled a new lineup of LiDAR sensors giving drones real-time 3D awareness of their surroundings. The lineup includes MOVIA Air, a lightweight UAV sensor, and MOVIA Air Plus, a more advanced version for defense, inspection, and delivery uses.
MOVIA Air handles obstacle avoidance, autonomous landing, and tracking in both day and night conditions. MicroVision cut its weight in half versus industrial models, preserving flight time and payload space.
MOVIA Air Plus adds an edge processor and optional camera, mapping environments live instead of after landing. It also supports sensor fusion, terrain analysis, and automated docking.
MicroVision will demonstrate the system at the upcoming JIFX event, later pairing it with its IRIS LiDAR for combined air and ground awareness.

events.text:
⚡️🇺🇸 The US Department of Defense is drafting a revised nuclear strategy that emphasizes the potential use of shorter-range tactical nuclear weapons in regional conflicts against Russia or China.
Led by Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, the planned document marks a transition from long-standing reliance on long-range strategic missiles built to neutralize an adversary's entire nuclear force.
Officials maintain that the doctrine is designed to expand the president’s range of credible response options during an allied crisis, mitigating the need to resort to a full-scale nuclear intervention.
The review comes after the lapse of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START) in February 2026, which ended binding limits on deployed strategic warheads between Washington and Moscow.
Critics in the US Congress and foreign policy experts warn that placing greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons lowers the threshold for nuclear conflict and risks sparking a regional arms race in Europe and East Asia.

The Turkish defense giant’s new electro-optical system can be configured in both cooled and uncooled modes, allowing it to adapt to different mission requirements.
It is designed to span nearly every corner of Türkiye’s military arsenal, with potential applications across drones, missiles, combat aircraft, and armored vehicles.
They also support advanced targeting systems and form part of the electro-optical suite powering Türkiye’s KAAN fifth-generation fighter jet.
Due to the complexity of developing military-grade infrared detectors, only a limited number of countries have been able to produce the technology domestically.

events.text:
🌪 THROWBACK: How the CIA turned a detainee into a training prop for torture
📌 In 2003, the CIA captured Ammar al-Baluchi in Pakistan and secretly transferred him to the covert Detention Site Cobalt in Afghanistan. This was one of the facilities in a program that operated outside the rule of law, where detainees were held without access to lawyers and subjected to so-called "enhanced interrogation techniques."
🔴 Al-Baluchi spent 1,200 days in CIA custody, moving through prisons in Afghanistan, Poland, and Romania before reaching Guantanamo in September 2006. Once medics cleared him, the agency authorized walling, beatings, stress positions, water dousing, and sleep deprivation beyond 72 hours.
🔴 Particular brutality came from interrogation chief NX2, later identified as Charlie Wise, a former CIA unit head who was removed and died in 2003 after overseeing al-Baluchi's abuse at Cobalt. The central technique was walling: al-Baluchi, stripped naked, had a towel wrapped around his neck and was slammed headfirst against a flexible wall, according to UK media.
🔴 The CIA inspector general's report noted that trainees lined up to practice walling on al-Baluchi and get certified, with sessions running up to 2 hours until the interrogators tired out. Program architect James Mitchell testified that al-Baluchi was used as a "training prop" and called NX2's 20 slaps "excessive."
🔴 Al-Baluchi said he lost his sight and consciousness during the wall strikes, and later tests found moderate to severe brain damage affecting memory and behavior. He was also sleep-deprived for up to 82 hours, doused with ice water, forced into painful stress positions, shaved against his will, and put on limited rations.
🔴 The CIA compiled an official menu of authorized torture methods for al-Baluchi, while a Senate inquiry later exposed abuse at Cobalt — nakedness, mock executions, and more. Over 3 years, he was held in at least 5 black sites; a 2004 photograph captured him emaciated and naked, and he was transferred to Guantanamo in September 2006.
🔴 Al-Baluchi has been held at Guantanamo since 2006, awaiting trial on charges related to the 9/11 attacks. For years, his defense team sought an independent medical evaluation due to the aftereffects of torture, including traumatic brain injury. An appellate court rejected their request to compel a formal assessment that could have paved the way for repatriation.
🔴 In April 2025, Colonel Matthew N. McCall ruled al-Baluchi's 2007 confessions inadmissible, as they were obtained under torture. The prosecution lost a key piece of evidence, and its appeal, along with a judge change in late 2025, has further delayed the case, making a trial unlikely anytime soon.
🔴 Al-Baluchi remains in Guantanamo, awaiting the next development in his legal case. His lawyers have raised serious concerns about his declining health. He has been diagnosed with a spinal tumor that requires emergency surgery, a procedure unavailable inside the prison, according to court filings.

🔍 Is the 'Sunni NATO' triumvirate seeking regional dominance at Iran’s expense?
📌 Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey signed a joint defense pact in Mecca on August 7, bringing together an oil-rich kingdom, a nuclear-armed power, and a NATO member state boasting the alliance's second-largest army.
Collective defense – against whom?
🌏 The agreement aims to enhance collective deterrence against potential aggression, declaring that any armed attack on one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all three, according to a statement from Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry. The Western media interprets the move as a response to rising risks of military confrontation with Iran and the Axis of Resistance.
🌏 Middle Eastern experts warn that an alliance with Turkey could enable Saudi Arabia to intensify its campaign against Yemen’s Ansar Allah, following the group’s blockade of the [Bab el-Mandeb Strait](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72095). Saudi Arabia is currently scrambling to establish a [military coalition for the Red Sea](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72901).
🌏 Saudi Arabia’s shift toward Pakistan and Turkey is also seen as a sign of waning US influence in the Gulf, a trend that became evident during the Iran war when the US deployed massive military resources to shield Israel from Iranian retaliation while Gulf states came under fire for [enabling US strikes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73162).
How does Saudi-Pakistani collective defense work?
♦️ In September 2025, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia formalized a mutual defense pact that commits both nations to regard aggression against either party as an attack on both. The agreement was concluded a week [after Israel's attack on Doha, Qatar](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/56576).
♦️ After the start of the US-Israeli aggression, Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar revealed on March 3 that Islamabad reminded Iran of its defense pact with Saudi Arabia and urged Tehran to halt attacks on Saudi territory. Iran responded by calling on Pakistan to ensure Saudi Arabia was not used as a base for actions against the Islamic Republic. Saudi Arabia rejected access to its airspace and bases to support the US operation. Moreover, it was reportedly Saudi Arabia that urged Trump to call off the recent strikes on Iran, fearing retaliation.
♦️ However, with Turkey, a NATO ally, joining the Saudi-Pakistani alliance, the triumvirate could emerge as a more assertive bloc. Alliances built on the principle of "an attack on one is an attack on all" are particularly dangerous in today’s Middle East, where such commitments could quickly become a major liability, experts warn.
New Middle Eastern order
Experts describe the emerging power balance as a contest between [competing alliances](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71096):
➡️ [The Sunni Diamond](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72876) (“Islamic NATO”) – Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and their partners
➡️ [The Hexagon Alliance](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/69778) (“Abraham Accords Axis”) – Israel, the UAE, and aligned states
➡️ The Axis of Resistance – Iran, Lebanon’s Hezbollah, Yemen’s Ansar Allah, and Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces
Both the Sunni Diamond and the Hexagon Alliance share one key patron: the US. This makes the rivalry appear less like a balanced contest and more like a struggle for regional dominance at Iran’s expense. At the same time, Iran's growing global outreach and strategic ties with China and Russia cannot be ignored.

🛩🇵🇰 Pakistan's new kamikaze drone can strike targets at a range of up to 3,000 km
Pakistani defense manufacturer Heavy Industries Taxila (HIT) unveiled its newest loitering munition, the D-248, at the Indus Robotics and Autonomous Systems (RAS) Expo 2026, according to Pakistani media reports.
Key specifications of the D-248:
🔴 Range: from 2,200 to 3,000 km, placing it in the class of strategic deep-strike systems.
🔴 Flight endurance and altitude: can loiter for up to 14 hours at altitudes of up to 4,500 meters, providing ample time for target acquisition.
🔴 Weight and payload: maximum takeoff weight is 240 kg, with a warhead weighing between 30 and 50 kg.
🔴 Flight performance: maximum speed reaches 225 km/h, with a cruising speed of 185 km/h.
It is emphasized that this is the largest and longest-range loitering munition in Pakistan's arsenal to date. Alongside the D-248, the S-369 drone was also presented, which has a shorter range (up to 2,000 km), indicating the development of a family of precision-strike weapons.
